fields.title: Describe the customer through their job, not their age
fields.keyTakeaway: A useful customer profile consists of jobs, pains, and gains. Demographics belong in it only if they change behavior—and they almost never do.
fields.checkQuestion: “Cafe owners, 30–45 years old, small business.” Which of this will be useful during design?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **who is our customer?** In block D1, we figured out what happens in the product; here, we look at who this person is and why they act the way they do.
fields.blocks/1/text: Recall our ongoing example: Smena is a shift scheduling service for small cafes and stores. The owner pays; the owner and employees use it.
fields.blocks/2/text: **What happens if you don't answer the question.** You get a persona like “Irina, 34 years old, coffee shop owner, loves order.” You cannot derive a single decision from this: any screen fits and doesn't fit such a description equally well.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Three parts, all observable and verifiable
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **Jobs**—what the person is trying to do: functional, social, emotional.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Pains**—what gets in the way, what they fear, what costs too much.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **Gains**—how they know things got better. Not “convenience,” but an observable outcome.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **Check:** every item must be backed by something you saw or heard, not assumed.
fields.blocks/4/text:
Useless: “Irina, 34, owner of a two-location coffee shop, values simplicity.”

Useful:
Jobs—fill the schedule for the week by Sunday; avoid running out of baristas on Saturday; send monthly hours to the accountant.
Pains—employees swap shifts in messenger chats without telling her; calculating hours manually led to a mistake and an argument once.
Gains—by Sunday evening the schedule is set and nobody DMs her.

The second description clearly shows what to measure and build. The first one doesn't.
fields.blocks/4/title: Smena: two descriptions of one owner
fields.blocks/5/text: A cafe owner's age changes nothing. But the number of locations changes everything: with one location, the schedule stays in their head; with five, it doesn't.
fields.blocks/5/title: Demographics belong in the profile only if they change behavior
fields.blocks/6/text: A profile is a generalization, so it always contains assumptions. Mark what is backed by observation and what is an assumption: six months from now, distinguishing them will be impossible. Also, a profile describes a person, not a situation—the same person behaves differently under schedule panic versus calm conditions.
